description:
Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
«Стань детективом трендов системы Земли!»
Проект: DAIRN — Great Steppe
Основная идея: исследовать долгосрочные изменения степных ландшафтов на основе открытых спутниковых данных NASA и превращать результаты в интерактивные природные карты.
summary: Steppe Jukebox is an interactive map that turns NASA Earth Information Center vegetation imagery into sound along virtual routes through the Kazakh steppe. Choose a date and play a route: as the map highlights each cell, the app plays a note based on its vegetation class. If usable data are missing, the app highlights the cell but plays no note. This brief silence marks a data gap, not sparse vegetation. By pairing NASA imagery with sound generated for the selected route, Steppe Jukebox answers the Earth Information Jukebox challenge and gives people a way to explore satellite data without relying on map colors alone.
details:
Where the idea came from. During a science lesson, fourth-grade pupils working with a paper map proposed representing it as a grid of squares. We brought their idea into the app and gave the grid a second purpose: the route through the squares becomes a musical score. Choosing a different route changes which squares you hear.

How it works. Choose Kostanay or Akmola, a data source, and a date. Play a preset route or choose one to five points on the regional grid to build your own. The app samples the selected satellite image along the route and maps five vegetation color classes to C4, D4, E4, G4, and A4. As the route plays, the map highlights each square in turn. A square with no usable data is still highlighted for one beat, but no note plays.

Why it matters. A low note means a low vegetation class; silence means the app had no usable data for that square. This distinction gives learners an audible way to spot data gaps. Pupils can also replay the same route using the same source on a different date and discuss what they hear and see. The app is an exploration tool: two dates alone do not establish a long-term trend.

Tools and design choices. We built the web app with Python and Streamlit. It interprets each satellite source using that source’s own legend, so the same note does not necessarily represent the same numerical NDVI value across sources. The sound is generated from the selected route and imagery, not from a prerecorded soundtrack.
